advisoryFindings.problem: The question tests a distinction between global extreme-poverty and rich-country poverty lines that the chapter never teaches, so the intended answer is not derivable from the lesson itself.
advisoryFindings.evidence: “Extreme poverty uses a far lower global line than many rich-country poverty measures.”

advisoryFindings.problem: The mortality-to-survival reframing is reasonably inferable, but it is not explicitly explained or demonstrated in the chapter.
advisoryFindings.evidence: “The same data now frames movement upward, which can make progress easier to see.”

advisoryFindings.problem: The minute-by-minute training-room setup feels mechanically generated and weakens the otherwise authored voice.
advisoryFindings.evidence: “At 8:05 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-6”

advisoryFindings.problem: Several examples restate the same bubble-chart and child-mortality material instead of adding distinct applications of the skill.
advisoryFindings.evidence: “Use the second chart to locate the largest group before naming the world.”

advisoryFindings.problem: The scenario shifts abruptly from a manager to a teacher, creating a small but noticeable continuity error.
advisoryFindings.evidence: “A manager at a board review applies the gap instinct before answering. The teacher sees the 1965 chart”

escalationSignals.problem: The precise percentage is presented without on-page sourcing or explanation.
escalationSignals.evidence: “the old rich/poor split missed the 68% in the middle.”

escalationSignals.problem: The country mortality figures and elapsed-time comparison are specific real-world claims that cannot be verified from the document alone.
escalationSignals.evidence: “Sweden needed 77 years, from 1869 to 1946, to get below 35 child deaths per 1,000 births.”

escalationSignals.problem: The account attributes a terminology change to a World Bank lecture and blog without identifying the lecture or post on-page.
escalationSignals.evidence: “A later World Bank blog announced plans to phase that wording out.”

escalationSignals.problem: The income thresholds are presented as definitive levels without an on-page date, currency basis, or source.
escalationSignals.evidence: “Level 1: less than $2 per day. Level 2: $2-$8 per day. Level 3: $8-$32 per day. Level 4: more than $32 per day.”

wrongQuizDetail: Each question has one clearly preferable lettered answer. Questions 6 and 7 are weakly grounded in the taught material, especially Question 6, but their distractors do not create multiple equally defensible answers or leave the questions without any defensible choice.
